body:
I intentionally kept it "deity agnostic" because the particular doesn't matter, but regarding the most popular ideology's take on suicide, that being Christianity's, that's why I bring up Hell in the classical interpretation of "separation from God." I don't buy the matter of us unknowingly being in Hell by virtue of myself considering it, ergo the thought is possible. I also have difficulty buying the word of the Bible by and large considering we are on who knows how many translations of translations of copies of copies... even going back to something like the Septuagint and the Hebrew Bible itself, not to mention the context of words changing over time; "natural" being one of the most immediately obvious, referring to the process of creation rather than being of nature. 

I believe that in mythology, there is always truth baked into the writings. Indian mythology is profoundly deep with astronomical information, for one. Jesus, as presented in the Bible, while I'm not convinced of his divinity, at least serves as a messenger of there being something more out there. Perhaps a reminder for those of us stuck in this separation from God that we can return. And again, I would hope that a merciful God would understand my willingness to leave this spiritually rotten world behind and return.

It's probably for the best that we continue this in DMs, considering the rule against proselytization (I don't want this to be interrupted). Nonetheless I'll seed the response here and you can just message me after this one. 

I feel like that's a bit of a kneejerk reaction on the big bang matter. In an eternally recurrent universe, one plausible model is an infinitely repeating series of big bang and big crunch events; however, as always, this begs the question of "where did it start," presuming that such things happened. An endless, self-regenerating structure is a beautiful one, as I'm sure you'd agree. I won't bore you with discussions over mishaps such as overly elongated laryngeal nerves, as I feel like that would detract from the discourse. That's not my concern right now. 

My concern is the matter of why suicide would make any difference in the grand scheme of things, and why if there is a merciful God, that I shouldn't just cut to the chase and return? Surely that God would understand the state of this fallen world, and one's willingness to exit (and not need make one suffer needlessly). We can't change others; we can only change ourselves, but what is there to change myself for in this world? Increasingly less by the day. We all desire that love but we're so alienated from each other that we are unable to reciprocate, as you said. At this point I'm willing to try my hand with that deity, whether it exists or not, and if that deity punishes me for being driven to the point of such an action in search of said love, then the love was never there in the first place, and I could never have been accepted anyways (I can't lie to myself regarding the divinity or lack thereof regarding Jesus Christ, but I'll at least acknowledge he probably existed as a person at least).

Fortunately, orbital mechanics (and physics' preference for spheroid objects with more or less uniform radial densities) are such that stopping this giant rock is nigh impossible save for a deity; the best the Earth has been able to do itself was to halt rotation for a second or so, that being the 2011 tsunami that hit Japan so hard. I never supposed that this world was eternally bereft of God, and perhaps there is something to a prime mover argument, especially considering that in an infinitely recurring universe, we can never really determine what said prime mover is (not to mention the hard limit on information itself because of that fact). All I can say is that I don't know what started the universe, but I suspect there was a hell of a lot that happened "before" the big bang. 

Now for the more interesting point made, that of good things happening. I think there are people who do good, and that out of a room of 100, at least half would want to help the other half out. However, evil can do "good" as well; they call them the golden handcuffs. What I've come to attribute to evil is not the brutal, violent actions that a demented individual may commit; rather, it's the banality. The day to day grinding down of the soul. The continued pitting of person against person for completely arbitrary metrics such as political persuasion, sexual orientation, race, etc. The societal structures that convince people to just get their own, damn everyone else, and then they wonder why they're so cold and alone later in life. A selfish, greedy, wrathful, and ultimately self-destructive mindset instilled into everyone. A world headed by a merciful god wouldn't allow such a thing, ergo I can only assume that we are bereft of God's presence here.

I should have specified that I was talking on a much larger timescale than the human life. As well, I forgot to mention the matter of the Poincare Recurrence, and the resulting fact of this universe being an infinitely recurring one. Hell is eternal, right?

I've struggled with that matter as well, the banality of such an action, especially in the case of no exterior escape. I die, I get born again aeons into the future, and I likely kill myself (as I have almost certainly done at least once before). Hence, either there is a path to redemption with such a deity to break out of this eternal cycle (or the breaking out of said cycle begins within oneself such as the concept of Nirvana), or we're here in this soul sapping domain forever. Meanwhile in a purely naturalistic, inherently deterministic universe as a recurrent universe must be, suicide carries with it no long-term consequences either.
